Successful protection and perpetuation of endangered species will have an impact on the interest of man. Man seems to have a special interest in the unique or unusual experience. The opportunity to see or hear a rare animal is no exception. The proposed action will result in greater attention drawn to endangered animals unique because of their rarity. This has moral and philosophical ramifications as well as direct and indirect economic impacts.
Many species will become first known to many people because of publicity that results from their rarity or because of actions of the program. A negative impact of the program will be the disturbing effect on the species when more people attempt to see it or collect it because it is rare. For example, announcement that an ivory-billed woodpecker had been located would undoubtedly cause a rush of well-intentioned people to see the bird for the first time. The intrusion could be harmful to the woodpecker. Some rare turtles and snakes are prized collectors' items. Addition of the species to the Secretary's endangered species list has been known to cause the demand to go up with a resulting increase in market value of the specimen. At the present time, a small population of an attractively-marked rattlesnake in New Mexico holds the fasination of collectors. Market prices go as high as $200 per specimen.
